claim: The feeding initiation circuit connects gustatory sensory neurons to proboscis motor neurons through three intermediate layers.
source: This circuit connects gustatory sensory neurons to proboscis motor neurons through three intermediate layers.
evidence: The abstract directly states this structural organization of the circuit based on the study's findings.

claim: Most neurons in the feeding initiation pathway are necessary and sufficient for proboscis extension.
source: Most neurons in this pathway are necessary and sufficient for proboscis extension, a feeding initiation behavior, and respond selectively to sugar taste detection.
evidence: The abstract summarizes experimental findings from optogenetic activation and inhibition experiments.

claim: Most neurons in the feeding initiation pathway respond selectively to sugar taste detection.
source: Most neurons in this pathway are necessary and sufficient for proboscis extension, a feeding initiation behavior, and respond selectively to sugar taste detection.
evidence: The abstract summarizes calcium imaging data showing selective responses to sugar.

claim: Hunger signals act at select second-order neurons to promote feeding initiation in food-deprived animals.
source: Pathway activity is amplified by hunger signals that act at select second-order neurons to promote feeding initiation in food-deprived animals.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental findings from optogenetic activation in fed versus food-deprived flies.

claim: The feeding initiation circuit is inhibited by a bitter taste pathway that impinges on premotor neurons.
source: In contrast, the feeding initiation circuit is inhibited by a bitter taste pathway that impinges on premotor neurons, illuminating a local motif that weighs sugar and bitter taste detection to adjust the behavioral outcomes.
evidence: The abstract summarizes findings from EM reconstruction and calcium imaging showing bitter pathway connectivity and function.

claim: Peripheral taste detection in mammals and insects is mediated by sensory cells that detect specific taste modalities and elicit innate feeding behaviors.
source: Peripheral taste detection in mammals and insects is mediated by sensory cells that detect specific taste modalities and elicit innate feeding behaviors.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Both mammals and flies have sugar-, bitter-, water-, and salt-sensing gustatory cells.
source: Both mammals and flies have sugar-, bitter-, water-, and salt-sensing gustatory cells (Liman et al., 2014; Yarmolinsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of sugar-sensing gustatory cells triggers feeding initiation.
source: Activation of sugar-sensing gustatory cells triggers feeding initiation, whereas activation of bitter-sensing cells inhibits feeding.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with implicit reference to prior work.

claim: Activation of bitter-sensing cells inhibits feeding.
source: Activation of sugar-sensing gustatory cells triggers feeding initiation, whereas activation of bitter-sensing cells inhibits feeding.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge with implicit reference to prior work.

claim: Mammals and insects evaluate internal nutrient needs with similar strategies.
source: Mammals and insects also evaluate internal nutrient needs with similar strategies (Augustine et al., 2018; Leopold and Perrimon, 2007; Nässel and Zandawala, 2019; Pool and Scott, 2014; Sareen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Neuromodulators released from neurosecretory centers and the gut signal hunger or satiety to oppositely regulate feeding.
source: Neuromodulators released from neurosecretory centers and the gut signal hunger or satiety to oppositely regulate feeding.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Disruption of hunger and satiety signals results in obesity and anorexia in mammals and insects.
source: Disruption of these hunger and satiety signals results in obesity and anorexia in mammals and insects.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Gustatory sensory neurons have been shown to be modulated by hunger signals and conflicting taste information.
source: Although gustatory sensory neurons have been shown to be modulated by hunger signals and conflicting taste information (Chu et al., 2014; French et al., 2015; Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; Jeong et al., 2013; Meunier et al., 2003), central mechanisms that modulate feeding decisions are unclear because the identity, structure, and function of central feeding initiation circuits are unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Central mechanisms that modulate feeding decisions are unclear because the identity, structure, and function of central feeding initiation circuits are unknown.
source: Although gustatory sensory neurons have been shown to be modulated by hunger signals and conflicting taste information (Chu et al., 2014; French et al., 2015; Inagaki et al., 2012; Inagaki et al., 2014; Jeong et al., 2013; Meunier et al., 2003), central mechanisms that modulate feeding decisions are unclear because the identity, structure, and function of central feeding initiation circuits are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that motivates the current study.

claim: Taste detection in adult Drosophila begins with activation of gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) found in sensory structures located on the body surface, including the external mouthparts, or proboscis labellum.
source: Taste detection in adult Drosophila begins with activation of gustatory receptor neurons (GRNs) found in sensory structures located on the body surface, including the external mouthparts, or proboscis labellum (Dethier, 1976; Montell, 2021; Scott, 2018; Stocker, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The axons of proboscis GRNs project to the primary taste and premotor center of the insect brain, the subesophageal zone (SEZ).
source: The axons of proboscis GRNs project to the primary taste and premotor center of the insect brain, the subesophageal zone (SEZ) (Kendroud et al., 2018; Miyazaki and Ito, 2010; Stocker and Schorderet, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The motor neurons that execute feeding have cell bodies and dendrites in the SEZ near GRN axons.
source: The motor neurons that execute feeding have cell bodies and dendrites in the SEZ near GRN axons, suggesting a local feeding circuit (Gordon and Scott, 2009; McKellar et al., 2020; Schwarz et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Only a few isolated interneurons have been implicated in feeding initiation.
source: However, only a few isolated interneurons have been implicated in feeding initiation (Flood et al., 2013; Kain and Dahanukar, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Fifteen second-order taste neurons and their synapses were fully reconstructed in the CATMAID platform.
source: Fifteen second-order taste neurons and their synapses were fully reconstructed (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) in the CATMAID platform (Saalfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology and results of EM reconstruction.

claim: The second-order neurons do not receive inputs from all candidate sugar GRNs.
source: The second-order neurons do not receive inputs from all candidate sugar GRNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); however, as sugar GRNs make extensive axonal-axonal connections (Engert et al., 2021), the impact of these differences is unclear.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data and cites previous work on GRN connectivity.

claim: Sugar GRNs make extensive axonal-axonal connections.
source: The second-order neurons do not receive inputs from all candidate sugar GRNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B); however, as sugar GRNs make extensive axonal-axonal connections (Engert et al., 2021), the impact of these differences is unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Optogenetic activation of seven of the nine second-order taste neurons elicited proboscis extension.
source: Remarkably, optogenetic activation of seven of the nine second-order taste neurons elicited proboscis extension (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation experiments shown in figures.

claim: Inhibiting the activity of each second-order neuron individually reduced proboscis extension to 50 mM sucrose in food-deprived flies, for six of the seven second-order neurons that elicited PER upon activation.
source: Moreover, inhibiting the activity of each second-order neuron individually, by optogenetic activation of the anion channelrhodopsin GtACR1 (Mohammad et al., 2017), reduced proboscis extension to 50 mM sucrose in food-deprived flies, for six of the seven second-order neurons that elicited PER upon activation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in figures.

claim: At a higher sucrose concentration (100 mM), neural inhibition of only two of the second-order neuron classes decreased proboscis extension.
source: At a higher sucrose concentration (100 mM), neural inhibition of only two of the second-order neuron classes decreased proboscis extension (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic inhibition experiments shown in figures.

claim: Multiple second-order neurons contribute to normal feeding initiation behavior.
source: These studies argue that multiple second-order neurons contribute to normal feeding initiation behavior and suggest that the partial redundancy of these second-order neurons ensures robust feeding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data on activation and inhibition of second-order neurons.

claim: The partial redundancy of second-order neurons ensures robust feeding.
source: These studies argue that multiple second-order neurons contribute to normal feeding initiation behavior and suggest that the partial redundancy of these second-order neurons ensures robust feeding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the circuit architecture.

claim: Proboscis motor neurons 4, 6, 7, and 9 are involved in extending different segments of the proboscis for feeding initiation.
source: Proboscis motor neurons 4, 6, 7, and 9 are involved in extending different segments of the proboscis for feeding initiation (McKellar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Motor neuron 9 (MN9) is necessary and sufficient for extension of the rostrum, the largest portion of the proboscis.
source: We focused on the well-studied motor neuron 9 (MN9), which is necessary and sufficient for extension of the rostrum, the largest portion of the proboscis (Gordon and Scott, 2009; McKellar et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The feeding initiation pathway is composed of interconnected second-order neurons and third-order neurons each receiving inputs from a subset of second-order neurons, and feedforward premotor neurons.
source: This strategy identified a minimal pathway from taste detection to proboscis extension, composed of interconnected second-order neurons and third-order neurons each receiving inputs from a subset of second-order neurons, and feedforward premotor neurons (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the circuit architecture identified through EM reconstruction.

claim: The third-order neurons include one previously characterized neuron, the putative feeding command neuron, Fdg.
source: They include one previously characterized neuron, the putative feeding command neuron, Fdg (Flood et al., 2013; Figure 3B), and a set of descending neurons, Bract, that project to the ventral nerve cord (Sterne et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bract descending neurons project to the ventral nerve cord.
source: They include one previously characterized neuron, the putative feeding command neuron, Fdg (Flood et al., 2013; Figure 3B), and a set of descending neurons, Bract, that project to the ventral nerve cord (Sterne et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The premotor neurons are strongly connected to MN9, representing approximately 13% of the synaptic input onto MN9.
source: The premotor neurons are strongly connected to MN9, representing approximately 13% of the synaptic input onto MN9 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: There are direct connections between three second-order neurons (G2N-1, Zorro, and FMIn) and premotor neurons.
source: There are direct connections between three second-order neurons (G2N-1, Zorro, and FMIn) and premotor neurons, and additional paths via third-order neurons to premotor neurons.
evidence: This describes the circuit connectivity identified through EM reconstruction.

claim: The neurons in the feeding initiation circuit are predicted to be cholinergic, except for Usnea and Phantom which are predicted to be GABAergic.
source: The neurons in the feeding initiation circuit are predicted to be cholinergic, except for Usnea and Phantom which are predicted to be GABAergic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), based on machine learning classifications (Eckstein et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions from machine learning analysis.

claim: Optogenetic activation of third-order or premotor neurons elicits robust proboscis extension.
source: Optogenetic activation of third-order or premotor neurons with CsChrimson revealed that each cell type elicits robust proboscis extension (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Acute inhibition of the third-order or premotor neurons with GtACR1 did not influence PER to 50 mM sucrose.
source: However, acute inhibition of the third-order or premotor neurons with GtACR1 did not influence PER to 50 mM sucrose (Figure 2E), consistent with multiple pathways to proboscis motor neurons.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Eight of the ten neural classes responded to sugar taste presentation in food-deprived animals, and not to water or bitter solutions.
source: Eight of the ten neural classes responded to sugar taste presentation in food-deprived animals, and not to water or bitter solutions (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data showing taste responses.

claim: Two second-order cell types responded to water taste detection: Usnea responded specifically to water and Phantom responded equally to water and sugar detection.
source: Two second-order cell types responded to water taste detection: Usnea responded specifically to water and Phantom responded equally to water and sugar detection.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data showing taste responses.

claim: Usnea and Phantom are reciprocally connected with GRNs.
source: Usnea and Phantom are reciprocally connected with GRNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these second-order cell types may tune GRN responses in the presence of water.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Usnea and Phantom may tune GRN responses in the presence of water.
source: Usnea and Phantom are reciprocally connected with GRNs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that these second-order cell types may tune GRN responses in the presence of water.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the connectivity and functional data.

claim: Fdg did not respond to proboscis taste stimulation, but did respond to optogenetic activation of sugar-sensing GRNs.
source: One third-order neuron, Fdg, did not respond to proboscis taste stimulation, but did respond to optogenetic activation of sugar-sensing GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Fdg may respond to pharyngeal or leg taste detection.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data with taste stimulation and optogenetic activation.

claim: Fdg may respond to pharyngeal or leg taste detection.
source: One third-order neuron, Fdg, did not respond to proboscis taste stimulation, but did respond to optogenetic activation of sugar-sensing GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that Fdg may respond to pharyngeal or leg taste detection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: High hemolymph osmolality is a key signal of thirst that acts on central neurons to promote water consumption.
source: High hemolymph osmolality is a key signal of thirst that acts on central neurons to promote water consumption (Jourjine et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Increasing hemolymph osmolality enhanced water responses in water-sensing GRNs.
source: We mimicked a thirsty-like state by increasing hemolymph osmolality, which enhanced water responses in water-sensing GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data in manipulated flies.

claim: In four of the five central neurons tested, response profiles were similar in food-deprived and thirsty-like flies.
source: In four of the five central neurons tested, response profiles were similar in food-deprived and thirsty-like flies (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data comparing different physiological states.

claim: Clavicle responded to water and to sugar taste detection in a thirsty-like state but only to sugar in a hungry state.
source: However, one second-order neuron, Clavicle, responded to water and to sugar taste detection in a thirsty-like state but only to sugar in a hungry state (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data comparing different physiological states.

claim: State-dependent responses to water at Clavicle may tune the responsiveness of the pathway to bias acceptance of more dilute sugar solutions.
source: These results suggest that state-dependent responses to water at a single node (Clavicle) may tune the responsiveness of the pathway to bias acceptance of more dilute sugar solutions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the calcium imaging data.

claim: The second-order neurons that receive sugar GRN inputs also receive inputs from candidate water and high-salt (ppk23-positive, Glut-positive) GRNs but do not receive inputs from candidate bitter or low salt (Ir94e) GRNs.
source: Remarkably, we found that the second-order neurons that receive sugar GRN inputs also receive inputs from candidate water and high-salt (ppk23-positive, Glut-positive) GRNs but do not receive inputs from candidate bitter or low salt (Ir94e) GRNs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data showing connectivity patterns.

claim: The connectivity is consistent with calcium imaging studies showing responses to sugar taste detection but not bitter taste.
source: The connectivity is consistent with our calcium imaging studies showing responses to sugar taste detection but not bitter taste.
evidence: This is an inference connecting EM connectivity data with functional imaging data.

claim: Responses to sugar and water were not consistent with the predicted connectivity for each neuron.
source: However, responses to sugar and water were not consistent with the predicted connectivity for each neuron, suggesting the possibilities of state-dependence, network interactions, and/or errors in GRN modality categorization.
evidence: This is an observation comparing functional responses with anatomical connectivity.

claim: Some GRNs may be misclassified, leading to errors in assessing sensory inputs.
source: As GRN category assignments in the EM dataset were based on anatomy and connectivity alone, some GRNs may be misclassified, leading to errors in assessing sensory inputs (Engert et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a caveat about the EM data interpretation, citing previous work.

claim: Hunger modulates sugar GRN activity.
source: Hunger modulates sugar GRN activity (Inagaki et al., 2012); however, whether sensory gating is the only mechanism for hunger regulation or whether modulation of central neurons contributes to an altered network state in hungry animals has not been examined.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dopamine enhances the sensitivity of Drosophila sugar-sensing gustatory neurons to promote proboscis extension at lower sucrose concentrations in hungry animals.
source: For example, dopamine enhances the sensitivity of Drosophila sugar-sensing gustatory neurons to promote proboscis extension at lower sucrose concentrations in hungry animals (Inagaki et al., 2012; Marella et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CsChrimson-mediated activation of sugar GRNs caused higher proboscis extension rates in food-deprived flies than in fed flies.
source: Indeed, CsChrimson-mediated activation of sugar GRNs caused higher proboscis extension rates in food-deprived flies than in fed flies, whereas activation of MN9 elicited the same proboscis extension rate in food-deprived and fed flies (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation in different feeding states.

claim: Activation of MN9 elicited the same proboscis extension rate in food-deprived and fed flies.
source: Indeed, CsChrimson-mediated activation of sugar GRNs caused higher proboscis extension rates in food-deprived flies than in fed flies, whereas activation of MN9 elicited the same proboscis extension rate in food-deprived and fed flies (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation in different feeding states.

claim: Activation of two second-order neurons, G2N-1, and Clavicle, increased proboscis extension in food-deprived flies.
source: Moreover, activation of two second-order neurons, G2N-1, and Clavicle, increased proboscis extension in food-deprived flies, whereas activation of all other neural classes did not (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation in different feeding states.

claim: Hunger signals act on sensory neurons to increase detection sensitivity and on a specific set of second-order interneurons to amplify sugar pathway activation and promote feeding.
source: Thus, hunger signals act on sensory neurons to increase detection sensitivity and on a specific set of second-order interneurons to amplify sugar pathway activation and promote feeding.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic activation experiments in different feeding states.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated that bitter compounds inhibit sugar-sensing gustatory neurons to prevent feeding.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that bitter compounds inhibit sugar-sensing gustatory neurons to prevent feeding (Chu et al., 2014; French et al., 2015; Jeong et al., 2013; Meunier et al., 2003), but have not addressed how downstream neural circuitry modulates appetitive feeding behaviors in response to bitter taste detection.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Scapula is a second-order bitter neuron which receives over 150 synapses from bitter GRNs and is the second-most strongly connected cell type with bitter GRNs.
source: We reconstructed neurons downstream of bitter GRNs (Engert et al., 2021) in the EM volume and identified a second-order bitter neuron, Scapula, which receives over 150 synapses from bitter GRNs and is the second-most strongly connected cell type with bitter GRNs (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Scapula synapses directly onto two feeding initiation premotor neurons, Roundup and Rounddown, but not onto second- or third-order appetitive taste neurons.
source: Scapula synapses directly onto two feeding initiation premotor neurons, Roundup and Rounddown, but not onto second- or third-order appetitive taste neurons.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Scapula is predicted to release glutamate.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Scapula is predicted to release glutamate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), which is often an inhibitory neurotransmitter in Drosophila (Liu and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This is based on computational predictions and citation to previous literature on neurotransmitter function.

claim: Glutamate is often an inhibitory neurotransmitter in Drosophila.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, Scapula is predicted to release glutamate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), which is often an inhibitory neurotransmitter in Drosophila (Liu and Wilson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Roundup responded to optogenetic activation of sugar GRNs but not bitter GRNs.
source: Roundup responded to optogenetic activation of sugar GRNs but not bitter GRNs (Figure 5B), as expected based on its response to taste compounds (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data with optogenetic activation of different GRN types.

claim: Upon co-activation of sugar and bitter GRNs, the Roundup response was dramatically decreased compared to the response to sugar GRN activation alone.
source: Upon co-activation of sugar and bitter GRNs, the Roundup response was dramatically decreased compared to the response to sugar GRN activation alone, arguing that bitter signals suppress the feeding initiation pathway.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data with co-activation of different GRN types.

claim: G2N-1's response upon co-activation of sugar and bitter GRNs was indistinguishable from its response to sugar GRN activation alone.
source: To test whether this bitter suppression reflects a central mechanism acting at Roundup, we monitored activity in a second-order neuron, G2N-1, directly upstream of Roundup, and found that its response upon co-activation of sugar and bitter GRNs was indistinguishable from its response to sugar GRN activation alone (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data with co-activation of different GRN types.

claim: Sugar and bitter tastes are integrated at feeding initiation premotor neurons, providing a central mechanism to reject sweet foods laced with bitter compounds.
source: Together, the EM and imaging studies demonstrate that sugar and bitter tastes are integrated at feeding initiation premotor neurons, providing a central mechanism to reject sweet foods laced with bitter compounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EM connectivity and calcium imaging data.

claim: The feeding initiation pathway is a local circuit, with three- and four-synaptic relays to motor output.
source: The feeding initiation pathway is a local circuit, with three- and four-synaptic relays to motor output.
evidence: This is a summary of the circuit architecture identified through EM reconstruction.

claim: Each neuron in the feeding initiation pathway elicits proboscis extension upon optogenetic activation.
source: Each neuron elicits proboscis extension upon optogenetic activation, demonstrating that each neuron participates in a pathway for the behavior.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic activation experiments.

claim: Inhibiting activity of single second-order neurons reduced the behavioral response.
source: Inhibiting activity of single second-order neurons reduced the behavioral response, whereas inhibiting activity of third-order or premotor neurons did not.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: Inhibiting activity of third-order or premotor neurons did not reduce the behavioral response.
source: Inhibiting activity of single second-order neurons reduced the behavioral response, whereas inhibiting activity of third-order or premotor neurons did not.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from optogenetic inhibition experiments.

claim: There are multiple routes between sugar GRNs and MN9 for proboscis extension.
source: These results are consistent with the circuit connectivity, which reveals that there are multiple routes between sugar GRNs and MN9 for proboscis extension.
evidence: This is an inference from the EM connectivity data and behavioral results.

claim: The multiple paths from second-order neurons to premotor neurons may enable proboscis extension to be recruited in different contexts to ensure robust feeding.
source: The multiple paths from second-order neurons to premotor neurons may enable proboscis extension to be recruited in different contexts to ensure robust feeding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the circuit architecture.

claim: Multiple circuit paths may enhance behavioral flexibility by facilitating sensory tuning and multisensory integration.
source: More generally, multiple circuit paths may enhance behavioral flexibility by facilitating sensory tuning and multisensory integration (Miroschnikow et al., 2018; Ohyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: EM circuit tracing of sensorimotor paths for feeding in Drosophila larvae revealed both direct GRN-motor neuron synapses as well as indirect pathways.
source: Consistent with our finding that there are multiple pathways for proboscis extension, EM circuit tracing of sensorimotor paths for feeding in Drosophila larvae revealed both direct GRN-motor neuron synapses as well as indirect pathways (Miroschnikow et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: G2N-1 was identified as a candidate sugar-sensing second-order neuron based on its anatomical proximity to gustatory axons alone.
source: G2N-1 was identified as a candidate sugar-sensing second-order neuron based on its anatomical proximity to gustatory axons alone (Miyazaki et al., 2015); here, we elucidated its functional role in taste detection and feeding initiation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and contrasts with the current study's findings.

claim: Fdg was isolated as a 'feeding command neuron,' able to elicit multiple steps in feeding, including proboscis extension.
source: Fdg was isolated as a 'feeding command neuron,' able to elicit multiple steps in feeding, including proboscis extension (Flood et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Fdg is a third-order neuron in the feeding initiation pathway, with synaptic connections to Bract descending neurons.
source: Our studies demonstrate that Fdg is a third-order neuron in the feeding initiation pathway, with synaptic connections to Bract descending neurons.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data showing connectivity patterns.

claim: Bract synapses with proboscis premotor neurons and ventral cord circuits.
source: As Bract synapses with proboscis premotor neurons and ventral cord circuits, Fdg and Bract are well-poised to coordinate proboscis extension with other steps in feeding.
evidence: This is based on EM reconstruction data and inference about functional significance.

claim: Fdg and Bract are well-poised to coordinate proboscis extension with other steps in feeding.
source: As Bract synapses with proboscis premotor neurons and ventral cord circuits, Fdg and Bract are well-poised to coordinate proboscis extension with other steps in feeding.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the circuit connectivity.

claim: Studies in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mammals have demonstrated that a key site of hunger regulation is at the peripheral chemosensory neurons, altering sensitivity of detection.
source: Studies in C. elegans, Drosophila, and mammals have demonstrated that a key site of hunger regulation is at the peripheral chemosensory neurons, altering sensitivity of detection (Chalasani et al., 2010; Kawai et al., 2000; Root et al., 2011; Savigner et al., 2009; Sengupta, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Hunger acts at a few critical nodes to modulate feeding initiation: sensory neurons increase detection sensitivity and second-order neurons amplify pathway activation.
source: These studies demonstrate that hunger acts at a few critical nodes to modulate feeding initiation: sensory neurons increase detection sensitivity and second-order neurons amplify pathway activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic activation experiments in different feeding states.

claim: Previous studies have demonstrated interactions between sweet and bitter taste modalities at the level of sensory neurons.
source: While previous studies have demonstrated interactions between sweet and bitter taste modalities at the level of sensory neurons (Chu et al., 2014; French et al., 2015; Jeong et al., 2013; Meunier et al., 2003 LeDue et al., 2016) and through feedback from the mammalian gustatory cortex (Jin et al., 2021), this study reveals a third circuit strategy for weighing sweet and bitter tastes: a local inhibitory network.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibitory interactions between bitter and sugar pathways at the level of premotor neurons provide an elegant strategy to weigh incoming sugar and bitter taste information and adjust behavioral probability.
source: Inhibitory interactions between bitter and sugar pathways at the level of premotor neurons provide an elegant strategy to weigh incoming sugar and bitter taste information and adjust behavioral probability.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional significance of the circuit connectivity and imaging data.

claim: By blocking activity at specific muscles, bitter detection may specifically change behavior to direct the proboscis away from a hazardous food source.
source: In addition, by blocking activity at specific muscles, bitter detection may specifically change behavior to direct the proboscis away from a hazardous food source.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of the circuit mechanism.

claim: The existence of a local inhibitory circuit for bitter-sweet integration has been recently postulated based on studies of mammalian taste circuitry.
source: The existence of a local inhibitory circuit for bitter-sweet integration has been recently postulated based on studies of mammalian taste circuitry (Jin et al., 2021) and may be a shared strategy across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature and suggests evolutionary conservation.

claim: Multiple circuit mechanisms for suppression of sweet attraction by bitter signals may reflect the evolutionary importance of robust bitter taste avoidance.
source: These multiple circuit mechanisms for suppression of sweet attraction by bitter signals may reflect the evolutionary importance of robust bitter taste avoidance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the evolutionary significance of the circuit mechanisms.

claim: Central modulation provides a strategy to bypass the limits of sensory modulation, allowing a broader range and different temporal dynamics of modulation.
source: As sensory modulation may suffer from finite amplification and incomplete suppression, central modulation provides a strategy to bypass those limits, allowing a broader range and different temporal dynamics of modulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of central versus sensory modulation.

claim: Seventeen candidate sugar GRNs in the right hemisphere were previously identified in the EM connectome by clustering GRNs using morphology and connectivity data and comparing the resulting clusters with immunostained GRNs responding to different taste categories.
source: Seventeen candidate sugar GRNs in the right hemisphere were previously identified in the EM connectome by clustering GRNs using morphology and connectivity data and comparing the resulting clusters with immunostained GRNs responding to different taste categories (Engert et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature describing the methodology.

claim: The 15 second-order neurons manually reconstructed receive 21% of sugar GRN synaptic outputs.
source: The 15 second-order neurons we manually reconstructed receive 21% of sugar GRN synaptic outputs.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: The distribution of second-order neurons has a very long tail, likely due in part to small neural fragments that are challenging to reconstruct.
source: We note that the distribution of second-order neurons has a very long tail, likely due in part to small neural fragments that are challenging to reconstruct.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EM reconstruction data and its limitations.

claim: Each of the second-order neurons is a local SEZ interneuron with arbors that overlap extensively with sugar GRN termini.
source: Each of the second-order neurons is a local SEZ interneuron with arbors that overlap extensively with sugar GRN termini.
evidence: This is based on anatomical analysis of EM reconstruction data.

claim: The third-order neurons represent a small subset based on comparisons to Flywire automated reconstructions.
source: The third-order neurons represent a small subset based on comparisons to Flywire automated reconstructions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on comparison of manual reconstructions with automated EM reconstructions.
